Moment Studios "Scraps" is like a mix of Interstate 76, Lego Racers and Stratosphere

I honestly feel like this is an example of what happens when the wrong press gets free keys to a game. Some people see it as a free pass to ignore objectivity and just say nice things.

Scraps has tremendous potential as an entertaining game with customizable vehicles and an interesting in-match upgrade mechanic. You pick up scraps (thus the name) from vehicles that you've damaged/destroyed during the match and then you can drive onto a platform that will teleport you back to your garage after several seconds so that you can repair and upgrade your vehicle before returning to the match. (Both repairs and upgrades cost scrap so if you're not really contributing, you won't be able to afford much.) It serves the interesting purpose of allowing players to make a trade-off...exit the match temporarily in order to return stronger. If you waste a bunch of time making the upgrades (or intentionally drag your heels and let your teammates pay the price), you'll eventually get outmatched by anyone who is making an effort to contribute and compete.

As mentioned in the article, all of the components you have with which to build out your vehicle serve a purpose. Generally, the more firepower you have, the more heating and/or generator power you need to keep it firing. If you don't have enough heat/generator power, the weapons shut down while you wait for them to cool down or for your energy stores to replenish. If you want enough cooling/generator power to keep a devastating array of weapons firing virtually non-stop, you're going to need to devote a lot of space on your chassis to those cooling/generator units, likely at the expense of other vehicle components like engines. It's a great way to provide players with a way to customize a vehicle to suit the way they want to play.

Having said all that, i have to take issue with the way that customization is portrayed. It's not like Lego so much as a freeform jigsaw puzzle being assembled on your choice of a fairly limited selection of premade chassis. You're not building out your vehicle with total control over appearances and the ability to fine tune performance. You put an engine in a spot where it fits and then you put other things in spots that fit and eventually you find yourself with odd gaps and spaces that are tough to use for the things you want. If you decide to try to build your vehicle defensively (ie. prioritizing protection of vital components as part of the design) the issue of finding a spot for everything gets even trickier. I'm not saying this is a bad thing. I don't think it's ever wrong to encourage players to think and exercise some problem solving skills to squeeze the most out of their creations. I just think the Lega analogy paints a picture involving more freedom than what the game actually provides.

The combat itself is quite straightforward, as it should be. You have guns and engines and wheels. Your opponents have guns and engines and wheels. You drive around and shoot each other until one of you can't drive around and shoot anymore. The components on the vehicles are modular and can be destroyed individually (ie. having your heat sinks destroyed by enemy fire will make your heat-producing guns take longer to cool off, reducing the amount of time you can spend firing continuously.) This goes right down to your scrap bins, another modular component that is necessary if you want to be able to collect any meaningful amount of scrap. Having your scrap bins destroyed means you're going to have a rough time funding repairs and upgrades.)

It really is a promising game, especially considering it's been developed primarily by one person. And it's still in development in an early access capacity so any rough edges will have plenty of opportunity to be polished smooth. The one thing that stands out as being in need of urgent correction are the engine noises. They sound like something you'd expect from an NES.
